newsitem.title: USA: U.S. government urged to takeover some D.C. finances.
newsitem.headline: U.S. government urged to takeover some D.C. finances.

text.p: The federal government was asked Thursday to assume more financial responsibility for the severe problems that have contributed to financial chaos, crumbling services and collapsing school system in the nation's capital.

The District of Columbia financial control board, established by Congress last year to oversee the city's management, issued a strategic plan that asked Congress to pitch in up to $1 billion each year to help Washington, D.C. stay afloat.

Among the programmes slated by the board for possible federal aide or takeover are D.C. prisons, Medicaid, mental health care and road and bridge maintenance -- services that most cities hand over to their states to finance.

"If we do not reach a workable solution together, we run the risk that the district will become a complete financial ward of the federal government," Stephen Harlan, vice chairman of the five-member control board, said at a news briefing.
Control board chairman Andrew Brimmer called the plan "our roadmap out of the district's crisis and into the future."
The congressionally appointed control board concluded that much of the city's financial strain is a product of its unique status, according to the report.

The district is not a state but must provide the same services as one. It pays for such expensive items as its own prisons and medical care for the poor while other U.S. cities pass along these costs to their state governments.
For most of its history, the 10-mile-square enclave that came to be called the District of Columbia was controlled by the federal government and Congress.
However, in 1974 Congress relinquished that power and awarded the district home rule and the right to vote for a mayor and city council.
"The costs that other states bear for their cities need to be borne for this city by the federal government," the control board said.

The plan sets 31 deadlines for major city actions between now and Oct. 1, 1998. For instance, the board will issue specific recommendations by the end of January for how to deal with the city's massive pension programme debt.
By the end of September, it will complete a report on how to finance the building and repair of roads, bridges and other city "infrastructure."
Also by the end of September, the city and board will make recommendations on how best to reorganize the city and the way services are delivered.

But a key congressional aide said Thursday Congress will not bail the city out until its leaders spell out more clearly what they want Capitol Hill to do and they do more to pare down an inflated budget.
The district faces a budget shortfall of $85 million this year, which must be met through further aggressive cuts in city spending and personnel.
